question: What is the maximum imprisonment term for an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
ground_truth: The person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both.
context: ...such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both.

question: Within what period must a cheque be presented to the bank for Section 138 to apply?
ground_truth: The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier.
context: the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier

question: If a payee receives information from the bank about a returned cheque but does not send a written demand notice to the drawer, can the drawer be prosecuted under Section 138?
ground_truth: No. Section 138 explicitly requires that the payee makes a demand for payment by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank about the returned cheque. Without this notice, the proviso conditions are not met and the section does not apply.
context: the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid

question: Does Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act apply when a cheque is dishonoured due to stop payment instructions issued by the drawer?
ground_truth: Yes. Section 138 can be attracted when a cheque is dishonoured on account of stop payment instructions sent by the accused to his bank in respect of a post-dated cheque, irrespective of insufficiency of funds in the account.
context: Section 138 of the Act can indeed be attracted when a cheque is dishonoured on account of 'stop payment' instructions sent by the accused to his bank in respect of a post-dated cheque, irrespective of insufficiency of funds in the account.

question: Why should a drawer of a post-dated cheque not be permitted to countermand its payment to avoid liability under Section 138?
ground_truth: Because allowing countermand would render Section 138 a dead letter and permit persons to take advantage of their own wrong. A post-dated cheque is an accommodation given to the drawer by the creditor, and the drawer should not be allowed to abuse that accommodation. Section 139 also raises a presumption that the cheque was issued in discharge of a debt, which the drawer must rebut with evidence.
context: A post-dated cheque will lose its credibility and acceptability if its payment can be stopped routinely... by countermanding payment of a post-dated cheque, a party should not be allowed to get away from the penal provision of Section 138. A contrary view would render S. 138 a dead letter and will provide a handle to persons trying to avoid payment under legal obligations undertaken by them through their own acts which in other words can be said to be taking advantage of one's own wrong.

question: Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, a presumption arises in favour of the cheque holder. What standard of proof must the accused meet to rebut this presumption, and must the accused personally testify to do so?
ground_truth: The accused must rebut the presumption on the standard of 'preponderance of probabilities', not proof beyond reasonable doubt. The accused need not personally testify: he need not examine himself and may discharge the burden on the basis of the materials already brought on record.
context: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. + An accused for discharging the burden of proof placed upon him under a statute need not examine himself. He may discharge his burden on the basis of the materials already brought on record... whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of the accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'.

question: According to Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde as cited in Rangappa vs Sri Mohan, does Section 139 raise a presumption about the existence of a legally enforceable debt?
ground_truth: No. Section 139 only raises a presumption that the cheque was issued for the discharge of any debt or other liability. The existence of a legally recoverable debt itself is not a matter of presumption under Section 139.
context: Section 139 of the Act merely raises a presumption in regard to the second aspect of the matter. Existence of legally recoverable debt is not a matter of presumption under Section 139 of the Act. It merely raises a presumption in favour of a holder of the cheque that the same has been issued for discharge of any debt or other liability.

question: What does Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act presume about a cheque holder?
ground_truth: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability.
context: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability.

question: Under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, who is deemed guilty when a company commits an offence under Section 138?
ground_truth: Every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company itself, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.
context: If the person committing an offence under section 138 is a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

question: Under Section 141, what must a person prove to escape liability for a company's offence under Section 138?
ground_truth: The person must prove either that the offence was committed without his knowledge, or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.
context: nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any person liable to punishment if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge, or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.

question: A government-nominated director of a company is in charge of its business at the time a cheque bounces. Can they be prosecuted under Section 141?
ground_truth: No. Section 141 explicitly provides that a person nominated as a Director of a company by virtue of holding any office or employment in the Central Government, State Government, or a financial corporation owned or controlled by either government shall not be liable for prosecution under that chapter.
context: where a person is nominated as a Director of a company by virtue of his holding any office or employment in the Central Government or State Government or a financial corporation owned or controlled by the Central Government or the State Government, as the case may be, he shall not be liable for prosecution under this Chapter.

question: Under Section 142(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, which court has territorial jurisdiction to try an offence under Section 138 when the cheque is delivered for collection through an account?
ground_truth: The court within whose local jurisdiction the branch of the bank where the payee or holder in due course maintains the account is situated shall have jurisdiction.
context: The offence under section 138 shall be inquired into and tried only by a court within whose local jurisdiction — if the cheque is delivered for collection through an account, the branch of the bank where the payee or holder in due course, as the case may be, maintains the account, is situated.

question: In Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod, the complainant argued that a contractual clause restricting jurisdiction to Aurangabad courts and the fact that the statutory notice was sent from Aurangabad should give JMFC Aurangabad jurisdiction. Did the court accept this?
ground_truth: No. The court held that principles of cause of action in civil law are not relevant in criminal prosecution. The clause restricting jurisdiction to Aurangabad courts has no bearing on the situs in criminal prosecutions, and the High Court had erred in analyzing the cause of action and the jurisdiction covenant as these are relevant only for civil disputes.
context: The principles pertaining to the cause of action as perceived in civil law are not relevant in criminal prosecution. Whilst the clause restricting jurisdiction to courts at Aurangabad may have efficacy for civil proceedings, provided any part of the cause of action had arisen in Aurangabad, it has no bearing on the situs in criminal prosecutions... the High Court committed an error in analyzing the cause of action as well as the covenant restricting jurisdiction to Aurangabad as these are relevant only for civil disputes.

question: In Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod, the cheque was drawn on a Delhi bank but presented at Aurangabad. Under Section 142(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, which court would have jurisdiction to try the offence?
ground_truth: Under Section 142(2), if the cheque is delivered for collection through an account, jurisdiction lies with the court where the branch of the bank in which the payee maintains their account is situated. In Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod, the cheque was presented at Aurangabad but the accused transacted business from Delhi and the cheque was drawn on a Delhi bank. The court upheld the High Court's conclusion that JMFC Aurangabad had no jurisdiction over the offence.
context: The offence under section 138 shall be inquired into and tried only by a court within whose local jurisdiction — if the cheque is delivered for collection through an account, the branch of the bank where the payee or holder in due course, as the case may be, maintains the account, is situated. + The High Court... concludes that the JMFC, Aurangabad has no jurisdiction over the offence described in the Complaint. The Appeal is accordingly dismissed.

question: In Icon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. vs Aggarwal Developers Pvt. Ltd., on what ground did the trial court acquit the respondents of the offence under Section 138?
ground_truth: The trial court held that at the time the cheques were issued, no legally enforceable liability had arisen because the conditions under the agreements to sell had not been fulfilled, the NOC had not been obtained by the villagers, and the legal notice did not appear to have been properly served on the accused persons.
context: at the time when the cheques in question were issued no legally enforceable liability arose. It was concluded by the learned trial Court that the cheques were not issued for discharging of legal enforceable liability. Finally, the trial Court also held that the legal notice did not appear to be served upon the address of the accused persons and, therefore, there was no proper service of the notice upon them under Section 138 NI Act. Consequently, the Respondents were acquitted of the offence under Section 138 NI Act.

question: In Icon Buildcon, the court held that ADPL's stop payment instructions were bona fide. What facts supported this conclusion?
ground_truth: The court found that IBPL was aware even on the date of the agreement that the properties were subject to litigation. A restraint order had been passed by the SDM on 16 January 2007 restraining the villagers from creating third party interest, and a further restraint order was passed by the High Court on 5 March 2007. Since IBPL's rights to the land were inchoate and contingent on obligations that were never fulfilled, it was not possible for IBPL to convey valid transferable rights to ADPL, making the stop payment instructions bona fide.
context: the depositions of CW-1 and CW-4 reveal that IBPL was aware even on the date of the agreement dated 24th February 2007 between it and ADPL that the properties in question were the subject matter of litigation... on the date when the cheques in question were issued, it was not possible for IBPL to convey to ADPL a valid transferable right in the properties in question... if on coming to know of the above difficulties, the Respondents had issued stop payment instructions, it cannot be said to lack in bona fides.

question: Section 139 raises a presumption in favour of the cheque holder. In Icon Buildcon, the cheques were dishonoured due to stop payment instructions — did this presumption protect the complainant, and what did the drawer need to show to rebut it?
ground_truth: Yes, the presumption applied. Even where a cheque is dishonoured on account of stop payment instructions, the presumption under Section 139 is attracted in favour of the complainant. It is rebuttable: the drawer can rebut it by showing, on a preponderance of probabilities, that the stop payment instructions were bona fide.
context: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. + even in a case of dishonour of cheque on account of stop payment instructions, the presumption under Section 139 of NI Act is attracted. However, it is rebuttable. The drawer of the cheque can seek to rebut the presumptions by showing on a preponderance of probabilities i.e., that the stop payment instructions issued were bona fide.

question: In Avneet Luthra vs Sunita Vijay, why was Accused No. 2 acquitted despite being a joint account holder on the dishonoured cheque?
ground_truth: Accused No. 2 was acquitted because he had not signed the dishonoured cheque. The court held that liability under Section 138 of the NI Act can be fastened only on the person who has actually signed the cheque, and mere status as a joint account holder does not attract penal consequences under Section 138 in the absence of a signature on the dishonoured instrument.
context: in the case of a dishonoured cheque drawn from a joint account, liability under Section 138 of the NI Act, can be fastened only on the person who has actually signed the cheque. Mere status as a joint account holder does not attract penal consequences under Section 138 in the absence of a signature on the dishonoured instrument.

question: In Avneet Luthra vs Sunita Vijay, the accused claimed the cheque was issued merely as a security cheque. How did the court address this defence?
ground_truth: The court rejected this defence. It found that the MOU dated 02.12.2021 expressly recorded that the cheque was issued towards repayment of Rs. 29 lakhs advanced by the complainant, and that the accused had signed the MOU after reading and understanding its contents. The court noted it was implausible that a cheque for exactly Rs. 29 lakhs was issued merely as security for future penalties, and that if that were the case, a blank cheque would have sufficed.
context: Ex. CW1/C expressly notes that the cheque in question was issued towards repayment of Rs. 29 lakhs advanced by the complainant... the accused persons have acknowledged that they executed Ex. CW1/C after reading and understanding its contents... It is also implausible that the cheque for exactly Rs. 29 lakhs was issued merely as security for future penalties. If that were the case, a blank cheque would have sufficed.

question: Section 139 raises a rebuttable presumption in favour of the cheque holder. In Avneet Luthra vs Sunita Vijay, once this presumption was activated, what did the accused need to do to discharge the onus, and did she succeed?
ground_truth: Once the presumption under Section 139 is activated, the onus shifts to the accused to rebut it on a standard of preponderance of probabilities. The accused can do so either by leading defence evidence or by specifying lacunae in the complainant's case. In Avneet Luthra, the accused failed to discharge this onus — she did not produce supporting documents such as bank statements, could not substantiate her claim that the cheque was a security cheque, and her admission of partial liability without quantifying it further undermined her defence. The court concluded she failed to create reasonable doubt in the complainant's case.
context: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. + once the complainant proves that the cheque was drawn/issued by the accused, the mandatory rebuttable presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act gets activated. As soon as the presumption is raised, the onus shifts upon the accused to rebut the presumption on the standard of preponderance of probabilities... the accused has failed in establishing a probable defence on a standard of preponderance of probabilities to rebut the presumption under section 118 and 139 of the NI Act.

question: What does Section 140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act say about a drawer who claims he had no reason to believe the cheque would be dishonoured?
ground_truth: That is not a defence. Section 140 provides that it shall not be a defence in a prosecution under Section 138 that the drawer had no reason to believe, when he issued the cheque, that it may be dishonoured on presentment for the reasons stated in that section.
context: It shall not be a defence in a prosecution for an offence under section 138 that the drawer had no reason to believe when he issued the cheque that the cheque may be dishonoured on presentment for the reasons stated in that section.

question: Are offences under the Negotiable Instruments Act compoundable?
ground_truth: Yes. Section 147 provides that, notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, every offence punishable under the Act shall be compoundable.
context: Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974), every offence punishable under this Act shall be compoundable.

question: Within what time should the trial of a cheque dishonour case be concluded under Section 143 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
ground_truth: Every trial is to be conducted as expeditiously as possible, and an endeavour shall be made to conclude it within six months from the date of filing of the complaint.
context: Every trial under this section shall be conducted as expeditiously as possible and an endeavour shall be made to conclude the trial within six months from the date of filing of the complaint.

question: What sentence may a Magistrate pass on a conviction in a summary trial under Section 143 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
ground_truth: In a summary trial under Section 143 the Magistrate may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year and an amount of fine exceeding five thousand rupees.
context: in the case of any conviction in a summary trial under this section, it shall be lawful for the Magistrate to pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year and an amount of fine exceeding five thousand rupees

question: Can the complainant in a cheque dishonour case give evidence on affidavit, and can the accused insist that the person be examined?
ground_truth: Yes. Under Section 145 the evidence of the complainant may be given on affidavit and read in evidence in any enquiry, trial or other proceeding. The Court may, and on the application of the prosecution or the accused shall, summon and examine any person giving evidence on affidavit as to the facts contained in it.
context: the evidence of the complainant may be given by him on affidavit and may, subject to all just exceptions be read in evidence in any enquiry, trial or other proceeding under the said Code. + shall, on the application of the prosecution or the accused, summon and examine any person giving evidence on affidavit as to the facts contained therein.

question: What does the court presume when a bank's slip or memo showing that a cheque was dishonoured is produced?
ground_truth: Under Section 146, on production of the bank's slip or memo bearing the official mark denoting that the cheque has been dishonoured, the Court shall presume the fact of dishonour of the cheque, unless and until that fact is disproved.
context: having thereon the official mark denoting that the cheque has been dishonoured, presume the fact of dishonour of such cheque, unless and until such fact is disproved.

question: By what modes may a Magistrate direct a summons to be served under Section 144 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
ground_truth: The Magistrate may direct a copy of the summons to be served at the place where the accused or witness ordinarily resides, carries on business or personally works for gain, by speed post or by courier services approved by a Court of Session.
context: a Magistrate issuing a summons to an accused or a witness may direct a copy of summons to be served at the place where such accused or witness ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works; for gain, by speed post or by such courier services as are approved by a Court of Session.

question: How is the law of a foreign country regarding cheques, promissory notes and bills of exchange treated when nothing has been proved about it?
ground_truth: Under Section 137, the law of any foreign country regarding promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques is presumed to be the same as that of India, unless and until the contrary is proved.
context: The law of any foreign country regarding promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques shall be presumed to be the same as that of India, unless and until the contrary is proved.

question: Under Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, within what time must a complaint for a Section 138 offence be made, and can a late complaint be entertained?
ground_truth: The complaint must be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138. The Court may take cognizance after that period if the complainant satisfies it that he had sufficient cause for not making the complaint in time.
context: such complaint is made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138 + the cognizance of a complaint may be taken by the Court after the prescribed period, if the complainant satisfies the Court that he had sufficient cause for not making a complaint within such period.

question: Where a cheque is made payable in a different place from the one in which it was made, which law decides what counts as dishonour?
ground_truth: Under Section 135, the law of the place where the instrument is made payable determines what constitutes dishonour and what notice of dishonour is sufficient.
context: the law of the place where it is made payable determines what constitutes dishonour and what notice of dishonour is sufficient.

question: If a complaint against a drawer is already pending in the court having jurisdiction under Section 142(2), where must later Section 138 complaints against the same drawer be filed?
ground_truth: Under Section 142A(2), all subsequent complaints arising out of Section 138 against the same drawer shall be filed before the same court, irrespective of whether those cheques were delivered for collection or presented for payment within that court's territorial jurisdiction.
context: all subsequent complaints arising out of section 138 against the same drawer shall be filed before the same court irrespective of whether those cheques were delivered for collection or presented for payment within the territorial jurisdiction of that court.

question: What does the expression 'debt or other liability' mean for the purposes of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
ground_truth: According to the Explanation to Section 138, it means a legally enforceable debt or other liability.
context: means a legally enforceable debt or other liability.

question: After receiving the demand notice, how long does the drawer have to pay before an offence under Section 138 is made out?
ground_truth: Fifteen days. Section 138 applies only if the drawer fails to make the payment to the payee or holder in due course within fifteen days of the receipt of the notice.
context: the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice.

question: In Sony George Kurian vs State of Kerala, why was the complaint quashed against the 2nd and 3rd petitioners?
ground_truth: Although the cheque related to a joint account maintained by all three petitioners, it was signed only by the 1st petitioner. The 2nd and 3rd petitioners had not signed it, so the drawer was only the 1st petitioner and the complaint under Section 138 was not maintainable against petitioners 2 and 3. The complaint was quashed to that extent and continues against the 1st petitioner.
context: though it is common ground that the cheque related to a joint account maintained by all the 3 petitioners, the cheque has been signed only by the 1st petitioner and the 2nd and 3rd petitioners have not signed the cheque and therefore, the drawer of the cheque in the instant case is only the 1st petitioner + the complaint for the offence under Sec.138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is not maintainable as against petitioners 2 & 3.

question: In Sony George Kurian vs State of Kerala, how did the High Court deal with the request to exempt the 1st petitioner from personal appearance?
ground_truth: The Court did not grant the exemption itself. It said it is for the 1st petitioner to make an appropriate application under Sections 205 and 317 Cr.P.C. and for the Magistrate to consider it, noting that under those provisions a Magistrate can allow an accused to make even the first appearance through counsel.
context: it is for the 1st petitioner to make appropriate application seeking personal exemption as envisaged in Secs.205 and 317 of the Cr.P.C. + by virtue of the provisions in Secs.205 and 317 the Magistrate can allow an accused to make even the first appearance through a counsel

question: In First Elearning Quest vs Tera Construction, must a complaint under Section 138 specifically allege that the cheque was issued to discharge a legally enforceable debt?
ground_truth: No. Relying on K.N. Beena v. Muniyappan, the court noted that under Section 139 the court has to presume that the cheque was issued for a debt or liability, so there is no requirement that the complainant specifically allege a subsisting liability. The burden of proving that there was no existing debt or liability lies on the accused, to be discharged at trial.
context: Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act the Court has to presume, in a complaint under Section 138, that the cheque had been issued for a debt or liability. + There is, therefore, no requirement that the complainant must specifically allege in the complaint that there was a subsisting liability. The burden of proving that there was no existing debt or liability was on the respondents.

question: How did the Delhi High Court dispose of the petition to quash the summoning order in First Elearning Quest vs Tera Construction?
ground_truth: It dismissed the petition as misconceived, with costs of Rs. 5,000. The court held that it was not a case for interfering with the summoning order at that stage because disputed questions of fact cannot be gone into in such proceedings, and it remained open to the petitioners to show at trial that they had not received the notice.
context: it is not a case of interference by this Court with the summoning order at this stage as disputed question of facts cannot be gone into these proceedings and it would be open to the petitioners to show that they have not received any such notice, for which evidence is needed. + The present petition is thus misconceived and it is dismissed with costs of Rs. 5,000

question: In First Elearning Quest vs Tera Construction, what presumption arises when a Section 138 notice is sent by post to the drawer's correct address?
ground_truth: A presumption of service arises unless the drawer proves that the notice was not in fact received by him and that he was not responsible for the non-service. This follows Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, under which service of a notice sent by post is deemed to have been effected unless the contrary is proved, a principle equally applicable to notices under Section 138.
context: with the correct address of the drawer written on it, it would raise a presumption of service unless the drawer proves that it was not received by him in fact and that he was not responsible for such non-service. + Section 27 of the General Clauses Act deals with the presumption of service of notice sent by post and provides that service of such notice shall be deemed to have been affected unless the contrary is proved.

question: In Anuj Gupta vs Praveen Kumar, why could the accused not be held liable under Section 138?
ground_truth: For two reasons. First, he was not the signatory to the cheque, even though it was drawn on a joint account, and liability under Section 138 attaches only to the drawer who signs the cheque. Second, the settlement agreement on which the claim was based was executed between the complainant and the accused's wife, not the accused, so no liability owed by the accused was shown.
context: accused cannot be trapped in the rigours of Section 138 NI Act for two reasons. + he is not the signatory to the cheque in question even though the cheque pertains to a joint account + the settlement agreement was not executed between the complainant and accused but between the complainant and wife of accused.

question: According to Anuj Gupta vs Praveen Kumar, when do the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act come into play?
ground_truth: Only when the signatures on the cheque, in other words its execution or issuance, are admitted. They are rebuttable presumptions, and they were not attracted in that case because the accused's signatures were not admitted.
context: presumptions under Section 118 and Section 139 NI Act take the forefront only when signatures on the cheque in question or in other words the execution or issuance of cheque is admitted. + The present case is not the one where presumptions under Section 139 read with Section 118 NI Act get attracted as signatures of accused are not admitted.

question: In Yogendra Pratap Singh vs Savitri Pandey, can cognizance be taken on a Section 138 complaint filed before the 15 days given to the drawer in the notice have expired?
ground_truth: No. The Supreme Court answered the question in the negative. No complaint can be maintained against the drawer before the expiry of 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice, because the drawer cannot be said to have committed any offence until then. A complaint filed earlier is not a complaint in the eye of law and criminal proceedings initiated on it are liable to be quashed.
context: no complaint can be maintained against the drawer of the cheque before the expiry of 15 days from the date of receipt of notice because the drawer/accused cannot be said to have committed any offence until then. + the complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act filed before the expiry of 15 days of service of notice could not be treated as a complaint in the eye of law and criminal proceedings initiated on such complaint are liable to be quashed.

question: After Yogendra Pratap Singh vs Savitri Pandey, what remedy does a complainant have if the Section 138 complaint was filed prematurely?
ground_truth: The very same complaint cannot be presented again at a later stage. The remedy is to file a fresh complaint. The Court directed that a fresh complaint may be filed within one month from the date of decision in the criminal case, in which event the delay is treated as condoned under the proviso to clause (b) of Section 142; otherwise the complainant must satisfy the court of sufficient cause under that proviso.
context: the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque may file a fresh complaint within one month from the date of decision in the criminal case and, in that event, delay in filing the complaint will be treated as having been condoned under the proviso to clause (b) of Section 142 of the NI Act. + the complainant cannot be permitted to present the very same complaint at any later stage. His remedy is only to file a fresh complaint

question: In M/S Laxmi Dyechem vs State of Gujarat, does dishonour of a cheque because the signatures do not match fall within Section 138?
ground_truth: Yes. The Court agreed that the expression 'amount of money ... is insufficient' in Section 138 is a genus, of which dishonour for reasons such as 'account closed', 'payment stopped' and 'referred to the drawer' are species. In the same way, dishonour on the ground that the 'signatures do not match' or that the 'image is not found' constitutes a dishonour within the meaning of Section 138.
context: is a genus and dishonour for reasons such "as account closed", "payment stopped", "referred to the drawer" are only species of that genus. + so also dishonour on the ground that the "signatures do not match" or that the "image is not found", which too implies that the specimen signatures do not match the signatures on the cheque would constitute a dishonour within the meaning of Section 138 of the Act.

question: According to the concurring opinion in M/S Laxmi Dyechem vs State of Gujarat, how are 'stop payment' cases treated where the account holder has sufficient funds?
ground_truth: As a category that is subject to rebuttal. The accused can show that the stop payment instructions were issued not because of insufficiency or paucity of funds but for other valid causes, including that there was no existing debt or liability in view of a bona fide dispute. Section 139 leaves the burden of rebuttal on the drawer, and it is an offence only if the drawer fails to discharge that burden.
context: the accused can show that the stop payment instructions were not issued because of insufficiency or paucity of funds, but stop payment instruction had been issued to the bank for other valid causes including the reason that there was no existing debt or liability in view of bonafide dispute between the drawer and drawee of the cheque. + the category of 'stop payment cheques' would be a category which is subject to rebuttal and hence would be an offence only if the drawer of the cheque fails to discharge the burden of rebuttal.

question: In Srimatha Mahila Sahakari Bank vs Aishvarya N, why was the accused acquitted even though the issue and dishonour of the cheque were proved?
ground_truth: For two reasons. The complainant did not comply with Section 138(b): although it knew the accused's correct and present address, it sent the demand notice to her old address. In addition, the complaint was filed without the signature of the authorised person. The court held that there was no commission of the offence and acquitted the accused.
context: the complainant even though very well know about the correct and present address of the accused and has issued demand notice to the old address of the accused. + even though the complainant has proved that cheque was issued by the accused and the same was returned for insufficient funds, but the complainant has failed to comply + Further the complaint is filed without signature of the authorised person.

question: In Rangappa vs Sri Mohan, did the Supreme Court hold that the presumption under Section 139 includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability?
ground_truth: Yes. The Court held that the presumption mandated by Section 139 does include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, and that to that extent the observations in Krishna Janardhan Bhat may not be correct. It is a rebuttable presumption, and it is open to the accused to raise a defence contesting the existence of the debt or liability.
context: the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. To that extent, the impugned observations in Krishna Janardhan Bhat (supra) may not be correct.

question: Why did the Supreme Court in Rangappa vs Sri Mohan agree that the accused had not raised a probable defence?

question: According to Rangappa vs Sri Mohan, does a reverse onus clause such as Section 139 place an evidentiary or a persuasive burden on the accused?
ground_truth: An evidentiary burden, not a persuasive one. In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden. The accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant to raise a probable defence, and in some cases may not need to adduce evidence of his own.
